To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) emergent groups can contribute valuable resources to disaster response and recovery that official organisations are not equipped to provide, 2) emergent groups are often more agile and flexible than official organisations in the use of technology to support their work, and 3) the use of ICT by emergent groups can be stabilised and institutionalised over time, but the process is not always linear and is often subject to political and economic forces.
the use of ICTs by the emergent, voluntary sector is an important and underappreciated aspect of disaster response and recovery.

the Cajun Army is an example of how unaffiliated volunteers use technology to fill the gaps in official disaster response and recovery, but that this emergent voluntary sector is not a replacement for the official response and recovery sector.

understanding the potential and limitations for ICT enabled, emergent, voluntary organisations to provide innovative, flexible, and agile solutions to disaster management.
the role of ICT in the emergence of the voluntary sector in disaster response.
how emergent voluntary groups can be better supported to contribute their unique strengths to disaster response and recovery.
